title: interpret multiplicity in f''
stem: A twice-differentiable function f on all real numbers has f''(x)=1(x−(-2))²(x−(1)), where -2<1. Which conclusion about concavity and inflection is justified?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both x=-2 and x=1 are inflection points because f'' is zero at each.
choices.rationale: A zero of the second derivative alone is insufficient; its sign does not change at the squared-factor root.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The graph changes from concave down to concave up at x=1; x=-2 is not an inflection point.
choices.rationale: Correct: The squared factor is nonnegative and does not change sign at -2. The simple factor changes sign at 1; f'' has sign negative then positive across that point.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither x=-2 nor x=1 can be an inflection point because f'' is zero there.
choices.rationale: A sign change of f'' at the simple-factor root establishes an inflection point even though f'' is zero there.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The graph changes from concave up to concave down at x=1, and x=-2 is not an inflection point.
choices.rationale: This reverses the sign of f'' on either side of the simple-factor root.

title: infer concavity from f' trends
stem: A function f is differentiable on all real numbers and f' is continuous. A graph of f' shows that f' is decreasing on (−∞,-2), increasing on (-2,1), and decreasing on (1,∞). No numerical values of f' are supplied. Which conclusion follows?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The graph of f is increasing precisely on the intervals where f' is increasing, and decreasing where f' is decreasing.
choices.rationale: Whether f increases depends on the sign of f', not whether f' itself rises or falls.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The graph of f is concave down, then up, then down on those three intervals; its concavity changes at x=-2 and x=1.
choices.rationale: Correct: Concavity of f follows the trend of f': increasing means up, decreasing means down. The trend sequence is decreasing, increasing, decreasing; only the stated changes in concavity are inflections.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The graph of f has local extrema at both x=-2 and x=1, because f' changes its increasing/decreasing trend there.
choices.rationale: A local extremum of f requires a sign switch of f', which is not given by its increasing/decreasing trend alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No concavity conclusion is possible without the numerical values of f' at the interval boundaries.
choices.rationale: The direction of change of f' suffices to infer concavity without knowing its numerical values.

title: exclude domain gaps from inflection points
stem: A function g is twice differentiable for all real x except x=0 and satisfies g''(x)=1(x−(-2))(x−(3))/(x−(0))² on that domain, with -2<0<3. The function has no value at x=0. Which statement correctly describes concavity and inflection points?

choices.label: A
choices.text: g has inflection points at x=-2, x=0, and x=3 because the displayed formula is zero or undefined at all three.
choices.rationale: An inflection point must lie on the graph; g is undefined at the domain gap.

choices.label: B
choices.text: g is concave down outside (-2,3) and concave up between the roots because the squared denominator is negative there.
choices.rationale: A nonzero square is positive, so it does not reverse the numerator's sign pattern.

choices.label: C
choices.text: g is concave up for x<-2 and x>3, concave down on (-2,0) and (0,3), and has inflection points at x=-2 and x=3 only.
choices.rationale: Correct: The squared denominator is positive wherever defined. The numerator has sign positive, negative, positive across -2,3; the gap at 0 is not a point on the graph.

choices.label: D
choices.text: g has no inflection points because its domain is disconnected at x=0.
choices.rationale: The domain gap does not prevent concavity from changing at the included points x=a and x=b.
